scenes.title: Key ideas
scenes.vo: What you actually get = quoted output minus price impact minus pool fees minus gas. AMM decks: you trade against a liquidity pool priced by a formula (Lesson 2.2). On-chain order book: orders matched by price and time, fully or partly on-chain. Aggregator: searches many pools and venues and may split your order across routes. Price impact: how much your trade moves the price. It grows with size relative to pool depth. Slippage tolerance: the worst price you'll accept before the transaction reverts.
scenes.cap: AMM DEX: you trade against a liquidity pool priced by a formula (Lesson 2.2). On-chain order book: orders matched by price and time, fully or partly on-chain. Aggregator: searches many pools and venues and may split your order across routes. Price impact: how much your trade moves the price. It grows with size relative to pool depth. Slippage tolerance: the worst price you'll accept before the transaction reverts.

scenes.title: Key ideas
scenes.vo: Routing: multi-hop routes (A to B to C) can give a better price but touch more contracts.
scenes.cap: Routing: multi-hop routes (A → B → C) can give a better price but touch more contracts.

scenes.title: Worked example
scenes.vo: Single pool direct, 59,100 U.S.D.C., $8, 59,092. Aggregator (split across 3 pools), 59,420 U.S.D.C., $20, 59,400.
scenes.cap: Single pool direct, 59,100 USDC, $8, 59,092 Aggregator (split across 3 pools), 59,420 USDC, $20, 59,400

scenes.sub: Selling 20 ETH: The aggregator wins by ~$308. Now selling 0.5 ETH: the aggregator quotes $3 better but costs $12 more in gas, so the direct pool wins. Big trades benefit from routing. Small trades mostly lose to gas.

lines: Why can an aggregator give a better price?
scenes.sub: Answer: It can split an order across pools, so each pool's price moves less.
scenes.vo: Why can an aggregator give a better price? ... Pause and think. ... The answer: It can split an order across pools, so each pool's price moves less.

lines: When does the best quote lose?
scenes.sub: Answer: When the extra gas costs more than the price improvement, which is common for small trades.
